overview: Borno developed west of Lake Chad as a centre of Sayfawa government and scholarship. Its history includes scholarly communities, farming settlements and changing dynasties, as well as royal capitals.

periods.title: Gazargamu and scholarly communities
periods.summary: Gazargamu became a centre of Sayfawa government and learning. Scholars established communities extending beyond the court.

periods.title: Pages designed for study
periods.summary: Annotated Qurans combined Arabic commentary with Old Kanembu translation. Their spacious layouts supported layered teaching and reading.

periods.title: Kukawa and a new ruling house
periods.summary: Al-Kanemi’s authority grew, with Kukawa as his centre. Sayfawa political power gave way to a new dynasty.

periods.title: Rabih’s occupation
periods.summary: Rabih’s conquest placed Borno under military rule centred on Dikwa. Demands for taxes, supplies and labour placed heavy burdens on communities.

periods.title: Colonial partition
periods.summary: European colonial partition divided Borno’s region among British, French and German administrations. The new borders cut across the older political landscape.

items.text: At Garumele, a settlement associated with Borno’s history, excavators found abundant fish remains together with sheep, goat and cattle bones. Oral traditions connect it with royalty, but its precise occupation dates and capital status remain debated.

The range and quantity of fish at Garumele suggest specialist fishing. Researchers propose that some fish arrived already processed, while herders supplied livestock. These are interpretations of bone distributions, not proof of a known market organisation or preservation recipe.

Nineteenth-century Borno depended on agriculture. Many people combined farming with seasonal crafts or trade. Kyari Mohammed stresses the importance of regional commerce alongside Saharan routes, challenging a picture of an economy sustained only by distant caravans.

Some scholarly villages combined study with farming and enjoyed royal exemptions. Students advanced from Quran memorisation to Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu translation and interpretation. Education rested on organised communities as well as individual teachers.

The Konduga Quran survives as loose leaves kept in a leather folder and satchel. Italian watermarks identify imported paper. Different hands added Arabic commentary and Old Kanembu glosses around the main text, preserving several readers’ work.

A later copy of the Konduga manuscript’s final page preserved its annotations as well as its Quranic text. The copy used a different page layout. This unusual duplication protected a record of teaching, not only the main scriptural passage.

Owners patched the Konduga Quran with paper strips and stitches after moisture damaged its lower margins. Repeated repairs show care across generations. A surviving manuscript can record maintenance and reuse alongside the original scribe’s achievement.

Extensive written annotations became less common during nineteenth-century upheaval, but handwritten Qurans and oral translation continued. Bondarev proposes links with political and educational changes; he does not establish one decree that ended the practice.

Rabih’s administration demanded produce and other revenues through local authorities under military supervision. Mohammed’s research describes confiscation and punishment as tools of rule. These burdens make the occupation a history of households and livelihoods as well as battles.

ending.text: Rabih conquered Borno in 1893. French forces and African allies defeated him in 1900; colonial partition followed. Royal institutions and regional communities continued under altered authority, while the independent state’s political order ended through successive conquests rather than a single timeless “fall.”
